extracted.intended_audience: aspiring cartoonists, comedians, and creative people who want to use drawing to make humor and solve personal/creative problems
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and practical criteria for making cartoons (especially autobiographical/comedic single-panel and short comics) that connect emotionally and solve or clarify personal problems. Covers idea capture, visual style, production habits, and the relationship between honesty and comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be distinctly and uniquely yourself
rubrics_metrics.description: Work should be 'distinctly and uniquely' the artist — authenticity is the most admired trait.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The host: 'the thing that ties everyone who I admire together... is that they found a way to be distinctly and uniquely themselves.' Aim for specificity and truth about yourself; the more specific and true you are, the more universally your jokes will connect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draw from personal truth / autobiographical material
rubrics_metrics.description: Use autobiographical material; drawing from your own life reveals relatable truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liana: 'It took a breakup to get me to start drawing more autobiographically... Drawing from my own life was a revelation... people could relate to me.' Use personal problems or events as raw material to diagram and understand them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use drawing as a problem-solving tool / diagram your feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat drawing as a way to diagram what you're going through to see relationships and move on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote: 'Drawing was my strongest problem solving tool, so I decided to diagram what I was going through.' When something is 'eating you up,' sum it up, diagram it, or sketch the dynamics to gain clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and impressionistic visuals over photorealism
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer simple, impressionistic marks and symbols rather than photorealistic detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liana rejects photorealism: 'I'm against that ideologically... who has the time to draw like that?' Simple visuals can be more direct and approachable; different visual thinking styles exist (photorealistic vs symbolic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on conveying emotion (body language, facial expression, symbols)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritize emotion in the drawing — use body language, facial expressions, or symbols to communicate feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liana: 'I care a lot about emotion, so if I'm using body language or facial expression or some kind of symbol to convey the emotion... that's all I need.' Omit extraneous detail that doesn't serve the emotional point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid clutter; include only what you care about
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not clutter drawings with elements unrelated to the core idea or emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consciously draw the thing you want to get across and 'not cluttering up your drawing with things that you're not caring much about.' Simpler compositions often communicate more clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two creation modes: problem-driven and free doodling
rubrics_metrics.description: Different mindsets: (1) draw to solve/express a specific problem, (2) make cartoons by freely doodling to let ideas emerge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you have something to work out, diagram it immediately; when you want to be a cartoonist, sit and doodle in an observational environment until ideas cohere. Each mode requires a slightly different mindset (direct vs exploratory).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capture ideas reliably (email/notes) and keep idea storage 'sacred'
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep a dedicated, easy-to-access place for seeds of ideas (e.g., email to self or separate idea inbox).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liana: 'I email myself an idea... experimenting with a separate email address just for ideas so that I don't have to see other emails.' Treat the space as sacred so ideas aren't lost or buried by daily noise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce regularly; separate generation and refinement days
rubrics_metrics.description: Be disciplined about making cartoons and schedule separate times for idea generation and for pushing/pulling (refinement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liana: 'I like to do the ideas all in one day and do the pushing and pulling another day.' Consistency (e.g., weekly submissions) helps maintain output even when ideas feel weak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterate: pushing and pulling is necessary to make an idea a good cartoon
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial doodles/ideas rarely equal finished cartoons — expect substantial revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Those ideas... it takes a lot more pushing and pulling before it's actually a good cartoon.' Allow time and multiple passes to refine timing, composition, and caption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use public/observational spaces to doodle and gather material
rubrics_metrics.description: Work in cafes, trains, or other places where you can observe people and scenes to seed cartoons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liana: 'I love to sit in a cafe or on a train... and then I'll just doodle.' Observing others can prompt ideas and character moments that become cartoons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technique/pen choice matters less than your voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't overvalue the 'perfect tool' — choose what allows you to speak in your normal voice visually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liana: 'Pen recommendations really don't transfer... if there's something that makes you feel like you're speaking in your normal voice... that's a good tool for you.' Focus on clarity of expression over gear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small, confident marks can be amplified (draw tiny then magnify)
rubrics_metrics.description: Draw very small, simple images and then enlarge them to make them read confidently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liana's process: draw 1–2 inch sketches, then photograph/scan and blow them up so they appear bold despite being drawn with a thin pen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy often requires a 'one-two punch'; honesty alone is a different effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand structural difference: a picture-as-setup plus caption-as-punchline is a two-part comedic device; a single honest image may be resonance rather than joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liana's theory: 'comedy is a one-two punch, and honesty is a one punch.' To be funny, often you need a shift or reversal after the setup; pure honesty can be powerful but not necessarily 'funny' in the joke sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep a lot of seeds; most will be worthless but a few will work
rubrics_metrics.description: Record many small ideas; only a small fraction will develop into good material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chris: 'in the course of a day... 30 things... most of them are worthless... a few of them are.' Systematically saving lots of seeds increases the chance of usable material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept repeating themes; use longer forms to avoid weekly single-panel repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that certain emotional themes recur; longer comics allow deeper exploration without constant 'newness'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liana: single panels can repeat and longer comics let you 'sink into one idea.' Repetition isn't necessarily bad; it can be authentic and relatable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow non-revelatory work; not every piece must be a revelation
rubrics_metrics.description: Relieve pressure to make every piece profoundly new; sometimes the value is in simply making the drawing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'If you put the pressure on the art to always have a revelation... sometimes it's not necessarily going to be revelatory, it's just going to be a drawing.' Regular practice matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use drawing to outline and externalize persistent personal problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Use comics to map recurring personal issues (social anxiety, relationships, gender expectations) until they become understandable or less urgent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liana describes using drawing to surface social anxiety, feminist rage, eating issues, dating — 'I outlined the problems for myself to the point where I don't need to keep outlining them.' Drawing can be therapeutic and clarifying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency over perfection when working to deadline or for a venue
rubrics_metrics.description: When you have recurring obligations (e.g., a weekly magazine), prioritize making and submitting work even if imperfect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liana: 'I owe The New Yorker a weekly batch of cartoons... if they're bad, at least I made them.' Regular submission builds momentum and opportunity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vulnerability connects — honest, small admissions can be the most authentic material
rubrics_metrics.description: Admitting small failures or blankness can create highly relatable work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Liana's 'If I'm Being Honest' comic about feeling blank — 'the most authentic ones' often come from confessing uncertainty or small humiliations rather than grand statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Track creative 'seasons' and save ideas for lean times
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware you have seasons of high and low idea flow; use your archive to pull material during low seasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chris: 'do you have seasons... how on earth do you save your ideas for the time when you need ideas?' Keep an organized idea repository so you can mine it later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use setup/picture + caption/punchline structure consciously
rubrics_metrics.description: For single-panel New Yorker-style cartoons, treat the image as setup and the caption as the pivoting punchline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liana: 'I always think of, like, a New Yorker cartoon with a picture that's a setup, and then the caption that's usually the punchline as a one-two punch.' Consider how image and text play off each other to create surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't overvalue technical mastery; strategic lack of polish can be an asset
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical virtuosity isn't necessary for effective cartoons; being an 'imposter' or unpolished can be protective and part of the voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liana: 'I take pride in being an imposter... it wouldn't even cross my mind to try to draw better.' Focus on communicative clarity; skill can help but isn't the only route to compelling work.
